hero.title: How to Compare Fancy-Shaped Diamonds When the Report Has No Cut Grade
hero.subheading: Use report measurements, proportions, polish and symmetry as a technical filter—then judge outline, light performance, spread, bow ties, windowing and durability by inspecting the actual stone.

paragraphs: Two oval natural diamonds can carry the same carat, colour and clarity grades while looking completely different.
One may appear bright, lively and gracefully proportioned. The other may show a heavy dark bow tie, uneven shoulders and too much weight hidden beneath the girdle.
If both diamonds have GIA reports, neither will currently receive an overall cut grade.
How, then, should a buyer compare them?

The answer is to use the report as a technical filter and the actual diamond as the final decision. Measurements, table percentage, depth percentage, girdle, polish and symmetry provide useful evidence, but they cannot replace an assessment of the diamond’s face-up outline, light performance, contrast, visible spread and movement.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer
quickAnswer.question: When a fancy-shaped diamond report has no overall cut grade, evaluate the stone through five connected areas:
attributes: Report accuracy: Verify the report number, natural-diamond identification, measurements and listed characteristics.
Outline and proportions: Review the shape, length-to-width ratio, shoulders, wings, corners, points and overall balance.
Face-up size: Compare the millimetre dimensions with diamonds of a similar shape and carat weight.
Light performance: Look for balanced brightness, fire, scintillation and contrast without severe windowing or persistent dead areas.
Durability: Check the girdle, exposed points, corners and inclusion placement.
closingParagraphs: Do not select a fancy-shaped diamond from table and depth percentages alone. Two stones with similar numbers can show different facet patterns, bow ties, windowing, brightness and face-up appeal.
The strongest comparison uses the grading report, high-quality video and professional visual inspection together.

keyTakeaways.title: Key Takeaways
items: As of February 2026, GIA gives an overall cut grade only to standard round brilliant diamonds in the D-to-Z colour range.
GIA fancy shapes still receive separate polish and symmetry grades.
Other laboratories may use different systems. IGI currently offers overall cut grading for fancy shapes.
Always inspect the exact report instead of assuming that every laboratory follows the same cut-grading policy.
Length-to-width ratio describes the outline; it does not prove good light performance.
Table and depth percentages are screening information, not universal approval rules.
Polish and symmetry do not equal an overall cut grade.
A small bow tie can provide normal contrast, while a large persistent dark area may reduce appeal.
Emerald and Asscher cuts should be checked carefully for windowing and uneven step patterns.
Carat weight does not reveal face-up size. Compare the millimetre measurements.
Extremely thick girdles and excessive depth may hide weight without increasing visual size.
Extremely thin girdle areas, exposed points and poorly positioned inclusions can create durability concerns.
Compare diamonds of the same shape, facet style and similar length-to-width ratio whenever possible.
The final decision should be made from the complete stone rather than one report field.

firstCheckLab.title: First Check Which Laboratory Issued the Report
introParagraphs: The absence of an overall cut grade has different meanings depending on the grading laboratory.

subsections.title: GIA Reports
paragraphsBefore: GIA’s February 2026 cut-grade guidance confirms that the standard round brilliant is currently the only shape receiving an overall GIA cut grade.
Oval, pear, marquise, cushion, emerald, princess and other fancy cuts do not currently receive an overall cut grade on GIA reports. They are still assessed for polish and symmetry.

This does not mean that GIA considers cut unimportant. It means that the variety of outlines, facet patterns and visual behaviour found across fancy shapes does not currently fit the organisation’s established overall cut-grading system.

subsections.title: IGI Reports
paragraphsBefore: IGI uses a different approach.
Its current fancy-shape cut-grading methodology evaluates polish, symmetry, proportions, craftsmanship and light return before assigning a cut grade ranging from Excellent to Poor.
An IGI fancy-shaped diamond may therefore have an overall cut grade even when an equivalent GIA-graded stone does not.

subsections.title: HRD Antwerp Reports
paragraphsBefore: HRD Antwerp reports can include cut-related information such as proportions, polish and symmetry. The exact information depends on the report type and diamond.
Review the actual document and the laboratory’s current methodology rather than treating cut terminology from different laboratories as automatically interchangeable.

subsections.title: Important Buying Rule
paragraphsBefore: Never compare an “Excellent” label from one laboratory directly with the absence of a grade from another and conclude that the graded diamond is automatically better.

bullets: Whether the grade is overall or limited to one component

comparisonProcess.title: A Practical Fancy-Shaped Diamond Comparison Process

subsections.title: Step 1: Verify the Report
paragraphsBefore: Use the issuing laboratory’s official verification system, such as GIA Report Check.
Confirm:
paragraphsAfter: The report details must correspond with the diamond being offered.

subsections.title: Step 2: Compare Diamonds Within the Same Shape Family
paragraphsBefore: Do not compare an oval directly with an emerald cut and try to decide which has “better” cut quality.
Brilliant-style fancy shapes and step cuts handle light differently.
Brilliant-style shapes include:
paragraphsAfter: These shapes often show more sparkle and faster patterns of light and dark.
Step cuts include emerald, Asscher and baguette diamonds. These shapes produce broader flashes and geometric reflections rather than the faster scintillation expected from brilliant-style diamonds.
Compare like with like: oval with oval, radiant with radiant, emerald with emerald, and cushion brilliant with a similar cushion facet style.

subsections.title: Step 3: Calculate the Length-to-Width Ratio
paragraphsBefore: The length-to-width ratio is calculated as:
Length ÷ Width = Length-to-width ratio
For example:
The ratio describes whether a diamond appears:
paragraphsAfter: It does not grade light performance.
GIA’s oval diamond guide notes that many buyers prefer oval ratios between approximately 1.30 and 1.50, but the most attractive ratio remains a matter of shape preference.
A beautiful oval can fall outside a popular range. A poorly performing oval can fall inside it.
Use ratio to match the desired silhouette, not as a substitute for inspection.

subsections.title: Step 4: Compare Face-Up Dimensions
paragraphsBefore: Carat measures weight, not visible size.
Two one-carat ovals may have different lengths and widths because their weight is distributed differently. One may carry additional weight in:
bullets: A hidden area below the setting
paragraphsAfter: Compare the millimetre measurements of stones with similar shape, carat weight, length-to-width ratio and facet style.
A diamond that appears unusually small for its weight requires closer investigation.
Larger face-up dimensions are not automatically better either. A shallow diamond may look wide but suffer from poor light return or windowing.
The goal is an attractive balance between spread, light performance and durability.

subsections.title: Step 5: Use Table and Depth as Screening Information
paragraphsBefore: Table and depth percentages help explain how the diamond’s weight and facets are arranged.
They should be used to:
paragraphsAfter: They should not be used as rigid pass-or-fail rules across every fancy shape.
An oval, cushion, radiant and emerald cut can use different facet arrangements even when their table and depth numbers look similar.
GIA’s research into oval, pear and marquise appearance highlights the range of outlines and visual patterns found within fancy shapes. This variety is one reason visual examination remains essential.

subsections.title: Step 6: Assess the Outline
paragraphsBefore: Outline appeal is one of the most important and least automated parts of fancy-shape evaluation.
Check whether the diamond looks balanced from above.
Look for:
paragraphsAfter: A grading report may state Excellent symmetry while the buyer still dislikes the overall silhouette. Laboratory symmetry and personal outline appeal are related but not identical decisions.

subsections.title: Step 7: Examine Light Performance
paragraphsBefore: View the diamond face-up under more than one lighting condition.
Check:
bullets: Dark areas that disappear as the stone moves
paragraphsAfter: A useful diamond video should show face-up view, slow left-to-right movement, forward and backward tilt, side profile, neutral background, diffused light and ordinary viewing distance.
A single highly illuminated photograph can conceal poor performance.

subsections.title: Step 8: Inspect the Girdle and Vulnerable Areas
paragraphsBefore: Check the complete girdle for:
paragraphsAfter: Pointed shapes such as pear, marquise, princess and heart require particular care.
An inclusion near a point or corner does not automatically make the diamond unsuitable, but it requires professional inspection and an appropriate protective setting.

subsections.title: Step 9: Compare the Total Price
paragraphsBefore: Cut quality influences appearance and commercial desirability even when it is not represented by one overall grade.
Compare:
paragraphsAfter: The cheaper diamond is not better value if its poor spread, severe bow tie or unattractive outline makes it difficult to sell.

lightPerformanceNoEquipment.title: How to Assess Light Performance Without Special Equipment
introParagraphs: Professional optical tools can provide useful information, but buyers can still make a strong initial comparison through structured visual observation.

subsections.title: Look at the Diamond Face-Up
paragraphsBefore: The central area should not appear consistently dull, transparent or inactive.
Brightness should be distributed across the stone rather than concentrated in one small section.

subsections.title: Move the Diamond Slowly
paragraphsBefore: Watch how areas alternate between light and dark.
Healthy contrast helps facets remain visible. A diamond that is uniformly bright under every angle may lack definition, while one that remains dark may have obstruction or leakage problems.

subsections.title: Change the Viewing Distance
paragraphsBefore: Some darkness is caused by the observer blocking light.
GIA’s oval guide explains that a bow tie can appear stronger when the observer moves closer because the head and shoulders block more light.
Evaluate the diamond at a normal jewellery-viewing distance as well as under close inspection.

subsections.title: Check More Than One Light Source
paragraphsBefore: Review the diamond under:
paragraphsAfter: Retail spotlights can make many diamonds sparkle. Diffused lighting is more useful for identifying uneven brightness and persistent dark zones.

bowTie.title: Is a Bow Tie Always a Problem?
introParagraphs: No.
Oval, pear, marquise and some other elongated brilliant-style diamonds may show a bow-shaped area of contrast across the centre.
A mild bow tie can add contrast and visual structure.
It becomes a concern when it:
bullets: Distracts immediately at ordinary viewing distance
closingParagraphs: Do not reject a diamond merely because some bow-tie contrast is visible.

windowing.title: What Is Windowing?
introParagraphs: Windowing occurs when the observer can see through part of the diamond instead of seeing light reflected back.
It is particularly important in step cuts such as emerald and Asscher diamonds.
To check for windowing:
bullets: Place it above a neutral surface or printed line.
Move and tilt the stone slowly.
Check whether the background remains clearly visible through a large central area.
closingParagraphs: A small amount of transparency at an extreme viewing angle is not the same as major face-up windowing.
A significant window visible when the diamond is viewed normally can weaken its appearance.

subsections.title: Oval Diamonds

Inspect:

subsections.title: Cushion-Cut Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Cushions vary widely.
They can be:
paragraphsAfter: Compare cushions with similar outlines and facet styles.

Inspect corner consistency, shoulder shape, brightness distribution, central pattern, dark or watery areas, face-up spread, depth, girdle thickness and whether the chosen facet style matches the customer’s preference.
One cushion may show broad, defined flashes while another shows smaller fragmented reflections. Neither style is automatically superior.

subsections.title: Radiant-Cut Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Inspect:
paragraphsAfter: Radiants can show strong sparkle, but some stones have uneven light return or excessive darkness through the centre.

subsections.title: Princess-Cut Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Inspect:
bullets: Brightness through the centre and corners
paragraphsAfter: Princess-cut corners are vulnerable and should normally be protected by an appropriate setting, such as V-shaped prongs.
A princess diamond can look bright while still carrying hidden weight. Compare its face-up measurements with similar candidates.

subsections.title: Emerald-Cut Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Inspect:
paragraphsAfter: Emerald cuts have broad, open facets. Clarity characteristics and weak optical areas may therefore be more visible than in a brilliant-style diamond.
Do not choose an emerald cut through table and depth percentages alone.

subsections.title: Asscher-Cut Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Inspect:
paragraphsAfter: A well-balanced Asscher should show an organised pattern that changes attractively with movement.

subsections.title: Heart-Shaped Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Inspect:
bullets: Girdle condition near the cleft and point
paragraphsAfter: Heart shapes are highly sensitive to outline quality. Small asymmetries can noticeably change the intended shape.

polishSymmetryNotEnough.title: Why Polish and Symmetry Are Not Enough
introParagraphs: Polish evaluates the surface finish of the facets.
Symmetry evaluates how precisely facets and shape features align.
Both matter, but neither alone measures:
closingParagraphs: A fancy-shaped diamond with Excellent polish and Excellent symmetry can still have an unattractive bow tie, poor spread or weak light return.
Treat polish and symmetry as important supporting evidence—not a replacement for overall visual evaluation.

warningSigns.title: Warning Signs That Require Closer Inspection
introParagraphs: Pause before approving a fancy-shaped diamond when you see:
bullets: Report information that does not match the stone
Unequal shoulders, wings, lobes or corners
Very poor face-up size for the carat weight
Surface-reaching inclusions near points or corners
Excessive colour concentration in one area
A video that hides the side profile or movement
A price that assumes premium cut quality without evidence
closingParagraphs: These signs do not always require automatic rejection. They require explanation, professional inspection and appropriate pricing.

subsections.title: Applying Round-Diamond Proportion Rules
paragraphsBefore: Fancy shapes do not use one standardised round brilliant facet arrangement. Round “ideal proportion” charts should not be applied universally.

subsections.title: Buying from Table and Depth Alone
paragraphsBefore: Similar percentages can produce different outlines and light patterns.

subsections.title: Treating Excellent Symmetry as Excellent Overall Cut
paragraphsBefore: Symmetry is one component, not a complete assessment.

subsections.title: Assuming Every Laboratory Uses the Same System
paragraphsBefore: GIA and IGI currently handle fancy-shape cut grading differently.

subsections.title: Ignoring Millimetre Measurements
paragraphsBefore: Carat weight can be hidden in depth or girdle thickness.

subsections.title: Rejecting Every Bow Tie
paragraphsBefore: Some contrast is normal. The concern is excessive, distracting and persistent darkness.

subsections.title: Comparing Different Facet Styles
paragraphsBefore: A crushed-ice cushion and a broad-faceted cushion should not be judged as though they are intended to look identical.

subsections.title: Trusting One Photograph
paragraphsBefore: A still image can hide bow ties, windowing, obstruction and weak scintillation.

subsections.title: Ignoring Setting Requirements
paragraphsBefore: Points, corners and vulnerable girdle areas must suit the planned jewellery design.

finalAnswer.title: Final Answer: How Should You Compare Fancy-Shaped Diamonds?
introParagraphs: When the grading report has no overall cut grade, do not attempt to create one from a table-and-depth chart.
Use the report to confirm:
closingParagraphs: Then use direct visual comparison to judge:
finalParagraphs: Compare stones within the same shape and facet family under identical viewing conditions.

The best fancy-shaped diamond is not necessarily the one with the highest polish and symmetry grades or the most popular length-to-width ratio. It is the stone that combines an attractive outline, balanced light performance, suitable spread, safe construction, reliable documentation and a fair price.

items.question: Why do GIA fancy-shaped diamonds have no overall cut grade?
items.answer: GIA currently gives an overall cut grade only to standard round brilliant diamonds in the D-to-Z colour range. Fancy shapes have more varied outlines, facet arrangements and light behaviour, so GIA reports polish and symmetry without assigning an overall fancy-shape cut grade.

items.question: Does IGI grade the cut of fancy-shaped diamonds?
items.answer: Yes. IGI currently grades fancy-shape cut quality using polish, symmetry, proportions, craftsmanship and light-return assessment. Its fancy-shape scale ranges from Excellent to Poor.

items.question: Can a fancy-shaped diamond be excellent without a cut grade?
items.answer: Yes. The absence of an overall grade does not mean the diamond is poorly cut. A fancy-shaped diamond can have excellent visual performance, spread, symmetry and outline even when its GIA report contains no overall cut grade.

items.question: Can table and depth percentages identify the best fancy-shaped diamond?
items.answer: No. Table and depth percentages are useful screening information, but they cannot confirm outline appeal, bow-tie strength, windowing, brightness or scintillation.

items.question: What is the best length-to-width ratio for a fancy-shaped diamond?
items.answer: There is no universal best ratio. The preferred ratio depends on the shape, setting and buyer’s visual preference. Ratio describes the silhouette but does not prove cut quality.

items.question: Does Excellent polish and symmetry mean the diamond has an Excellent cut?
items.answer: No. Polish and symmetry assess finish and alignment. They do not fully evaluate brightness, fire, scintillation, weight distribution, bow ties, windowing or face-up appeal.

items.question: Is a bow tie always bad in an oval or pear diamond?
items.answer: No. A mild bow tie can provide normal contrast. It becomes a concern when it is excessively dark, large, distracting and persistent during movement.

items.question: How can I check an emerald-cut diamond for windowing?
items.answer: View the diamond face-up over a neutral surface or printed line and move it slowly. Significant windowing may allow the background to remain clearly visible through a large central area.

items.question: Why can two diamonds with the same carat weight look different in size?
items.answer: Carat measures weight rather than visible dimensions. One diamond may carry additional weight in its depth, crown, pavilion or girdle and therefore appear smaller from above.

items.question: What is the best way to compare fancy-shaped diamonds online?
items.answer: Compare verified reports, millimetre measurements and high-quality 360-degree videos recorded under the same conditions. Request face-up, side-profile and movement views before completing the purchase.

finalTakeaway.title: Use the Report as a Filter—and the Diamond as the Decision
introParagraphs: Fancy-shaped cut quality is judged through outline, spread, light performance, durability and documentation—not a single missing cut grade.
Compare like with like, inspect videos carefully, and approve the stone that looks and performs correctly for its intended jewellery.
